factor_verdicts.new_wording: Race condition between DNS Enactors: a delayed Enactor applied an older plan after a newer plan had already been applied, overwriting it, because the check that its plan was newer ran only once before application began, not at each Route53 write. Contributing conditions: that Enactor experienced unusually high delays and retries while the Planner continued producing many newer plan generations, widening the window for an out-of-order apply.

factors.factor: Race condition between DNS Enactors: a delayed Enactor applied an older plan after a newer plan had already been applied, overwriting it, because the check that its plan was newer ran only once before application began, not at each Route53 write. Contributing conditions: that Enactor experienced unusually high delays and retries while the Planner continued producing many newer plan generations, widening the window for an out-of-order apply.
factors.evidence: "Before it begins to apply a new plan, the Enactor makes a one-time check that its plan is newer than the previously applied plan." and "the first (delayed) Enactor applied its much older plan to the regional DynamoDB endpoint, overwriting the newer plan." | "Right before the event, one DNS Enactor experienced unusually high delays and needed to retry its update on several DNS endpoints. While it was slowly working through the endpoints, the DNS Planner continued to run and produced many newer generations of plans."

factors.factor: Plan clean-up process deleted the active plan, leaving the regional DNS record empty and no Enactor able to apply subsequent updates.
factors.evidence: "The second Enactor's clean-up process then deleted this older plan because it was many generations older than the plan it had just applied. As this plan was deleted, all IP addresses for the regional endpoint were immediately removed, leaving an empty DNS record."

factors.factor: Automation lacked a self-repair path for the empty-record inconsistent state, so recovery depended on manual operator intervention, prolonging the DynamoDB outage.
factors.evidence: "The automation did not repair the record. Manual operator intervention was required."

factors.factor: Hard dependency of EC2 droplet lease management (DWFM) on DynamoDB, so the DynamoDB DNS failure cascaded into EC2 state checks and lease expiry.
factors.evidence: "DWFM state checks began to fail, because the process depends on DynamoDB." and "Between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM, leases between DWFM and droplets slowly timed out."

factors.factor: No established operational recovery procedure existed for DWFM lease re-establishment at fleet scale, so lease work timed out and queued retries prevented forward progress until throttling and selective host restarts were applied.
factors.evidence: "There was no established operational recovery procedure for this situation, and engineers took care not to cause further issues while attempting multiple mitigation steps." and "DWFM was unable to make forward progress in recovering leases."

factors.factor: Health check subsystem brought new EC2 instances into service before network state had propagated, causing alternating health check failures and removal of healthy capacity from DNS.
factors.evidence: "the health check subsystem brought new EC2 instances into service before their network state had fully propagated, so health checks failed even when NLB nodes and targets were healthy."

factors.factor: Degraded health check subsystem triggered automatic AZ DNS failover, removing capacity from multi-AZ load balancers and causing connection errors; the automatic failover had to be disabled manually.
factors.evidence: "The alternating results increased load on the health check subsystem, which degraded, delayed health checks and triggered automatic AZ DNS failover." and "Engineers disabled automatic health check failover for NLB"

factors.factor: Cross-service dependency on EC2 and NLB: Lambda, Redshift, STS, Connect and others were impaired by DynamoDB, EC2 launch, or NLB issues, widening the blast radius.
factors.evidence: "Clusters needing host replacement were blocked because EC2 launches were impaired." and "From 7:04 AM, NLB health check failures triggered instance terminations, leaving Lambda internal systems under-scaled"

action_items.action: Modify the DNS Enactor so every Route53 transaction verifies that the plan being written is newer than the currently applied plan, not only a one-time check before application begins.
Change the plan clean-up process so it never deletes the currently active plan or any plan that a live endpoint depends on, regardless of generation age.
Add automated detection and self-repair for the empty-DNS-record inconsistent state so the system recovers without manual operator intervention.
Add alarms on regional DynamoDB endpoint record count and on Enactor apply latency or retry counts, alerting on-call before DNS records become empty.
Reduce the EC2 DWFM dependency on DynamoDB so lease state checks can continue or degrade gracefully during DynamoDB endpoint failures.
Develop and rehearse a documented, staged recovery runbook for DWFM lease re-establishment at full fleet scale, including throttling and selective host restart procedures.
Gate health check subsystem admission of newly launched EC2 instances on confirmed network state propagation before they are added to NLB service.
Add safeguards so health check degradation cannot trigger automatic AZ DNS failover that removes large amounts of capacity, with a manual override that is tested in advance.
Remove the cross-region dependency of Redshift IAM user-group resolution on an IAM API in us-east-1 by making it regionally local or cached.
Audit critical services for hard dependencies on us-east-1 control-plane components (including EC2 launches and DynamoDB) and define cell-based or static-stability fallbacks for them.
Add a Lambda throttling and scaling safeguard so that loss of capacity in the underlying compute layer does not leave internal systems under-scaled after health check failures.
Ensure Lambda's SQS-polling internal subsystem automatically recovers after dependency failures instead of requiring manual restoration.
